body:
Why Aihole is important

Aihole, in present-day Karnataka, was an important early Chalukyan centre in the Malaprabha River region. It is especially significant for the development of Indian temple architecture.

During the Early Chalukyan period, builders at Aihole experimented with different temple plans, halls, pillars, roofs and towers. Both rock-cut and structural temples were constructed.

Aihole is consequently often described as a cradle of Indian temple architecture. This expression refers to its important experimental contribution, not to a claim that every Indian temple style originated exclusively at Aihole.

Durga Temple: An unusual apsidal plan

The Durga Temple at Aihole is particularly notable for its apsidal plan.

An apsidal building has a curved or semicircular end rather than a completely rectangular plan. This form resembles the rounded end of certain early Buddhist chaitya halls.

The Durga Temple combines this unusual curved plan with a surrounding pillared passage and a tower showing northern, or Nagara, architectural characteristics.

The name Durga is associated with the nearby fortification; the local name Durgadagudi refers to a temple near the fort. Therefore, the present name should not by itself be treated as proof that the temple was originally dedicated to the goddess Durga.

The monument is generally assigned to the late 7th or early 8th century CE.

Lad Khan Temple: An early hall-like design

The Lad Khan Temple is another important monument at Aihole.

Unlike a temple dominated by a tall tower, Lad Khan has a relatively low, broad, hall-like appearance. Its design includes a pillared hall and a sanctuary, showing how early stone temple builders adapted architectural forms resembling assembly halls and timber-roofed buildings.

Its present name comes from a later historical association and should not be interpreted as the name of its original builder or dedication.

Ravana Phadi Cave: A rock-cut Shaiva shrine

The Ravana Phadi, or Ravanphadi, cave is an early rock-cut shrine at Aihole associated with Shiva.

One of its important sculptures depicts dancing Shiva accompanied by the Saptamatrikas, or 7 mother goddesses.

Its importance lies in its rock-cut form and its association with early Chalukyan religious sculpture. It should not be confused with the Badami cave group, although both belong to the same broad architectural tradition.

Meguti Jain Temple: A dated historical monument

The Meguti Jain Temple stands on a hill at Aihole and is associated with the inscription composed by Ravikirti during the reign of Pulakeshin II.

The inscription is dated to approximately 634–635 CE, corresponding to Shaka year 556. The temple is important because it connects Chalukyan architectural activity with a precisely dated historical record.

How the different temples demonstrate experimentation

The monuments at Aihole do not follow one identical plan.

  • The Durga Temple demonstrates an apsidal plan.
  • The Lad Khan Temple demonstrates a comparatively low, hall-like structural form.
  • The Ravana Phadi shrine demonstrates rock-cut architecture.
  • The Meguti Temple is a Jain structural temple associated with a dated inscription.

These different examples help explain why Aihole is associated with architectural experimentation rather than one standard temple design.

Prelims focus

  • Aihole is in Karnataka and is associated with early Chalukyan temple experimentation.
  • Durga Temple: apsidal plan and Nagara-like tower.
  • Lad Khan Temple: early hall-like structural temple.
  • Ravana Phadi: rock-cut Shaiva shrine with dancing Shiva and Saptamatrikas.
  • Meguti Jain Temple: Ravikirti's inscription dated 634–635 CE.
  • Trap: The Durga Temple's present name does not establish an original dedication to the goddess Durga.

[NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 87–88; Government of Karnataka, Bagalkote District Administration, Aihole, sections Durga Temple, Ladh Khan Temple, Meguti Temple and Ravanphadi Cave, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Evolution of Temple Architecture – Aihole-Badami-Pattadakal, Tentative List Description, section Group of Temples in Aihole, consulted 18 November 2026; Government of Karnataka, Department of Tourism, Aihole, sections Introduction and Places to Visit, consulted 18 November 2026.]

body:
Pattadakal as a royal and religious centre

Pattadakal, in present-day Karnataka, was an important ceremonial and religious centre of the Early Chalukyas. The site is situated near the Malaprabha River and is historically associated with the coronation of Chalukyan rulers.

Its name is connected with this royal function. Pattadakal is commonly described as a place of coronation.

The temples constructed here during the 7th and 8th centuries CE represent a major stage in Early Chalukyan architecture. Whereas Aihole is especially noted for experimentation, Pattadakal is celebrated for the mature use of different architectural traditions.

Nagara and Dravida architecture

The temples at Pattadakal demonstrate the coexistence and interaction of northern and southern Indian temple forms.

Nagara tradition

The Nagara tradition is associated mainly with northern India. A characteristic feature is a curvilinear tower, called a shikhara, rising above the main sanctuary.

At Pattadakal, temples such as Galaganatha and Kashi Vishweshwara provide examples of the northern or Rekha-Nagara form.

Dravida tradition

The Dravida tradition is associated mainly with southern India. Its characteristic temple superstructure is a tiered, pyramidal vimana rising above the sanctuary.

The Virupaksha, Mallikarjuna and Sangameshwara temples at Pattadakal are prominent examples of the Dravida tradition.

What is meant by Vesara?

The term Vesara is used for certain Deccan temple forms that combine architectural characteristics associated with northern and southern traditions.

Early Chalukyan architecture is important because builders worked with different regional styles and sometimes combined their elements. However, this does not mean that every Chalukyan temple is an identical mixture of Nagara and Dravida architecture.

At Pattadakal, individual temples can still be identified as predominantly Nagara or predominantly Dravida, even though the wider architectural tradition shows interaction between the 2 styles.

Virupaksha Temple and Queen Lokamahadevi

The most celebrated monument at Pattadakal is the Virupaksha Temple.

It was constructed around 740 CE under the patronage of Queen Lokamahadevi, the chief queen of the Chalukyan ruler Vikramaditya II.

The temple commemorated Vikramaditya II's victories over the Pallavas. It was originally associated with the name Lokeshvara, reflecting the queen's patronage.

The Virupaksha Temple is an important example of Dravida architecture. Its design shows the influence of southern temple-building traditions associated with the Pallavas of Kanchipuram.

The monument is particularly significant because it connects Chalukyan military success, royal patronage and temple construction.

Other important temples at Pattadakal

Mallikarjuna Temple

The Mallikarjuna Temple was constructed under the patronage of Queen Trailokyamahadevi, another queen of Vikramaditya II.

It was built around the same period as the Virupaksha Temple to commemorate the Chalukyan victory over the Pallavas. Its earlier name was Trailokeshvara.

It is a smaller temple than Virupaksha but follows a broadly similar Dravida architectural tradition.

Sangameshwara Temple

The Sangameshwara Temple is among the earliest important structural temples of the Pattadakal group. It was built during the reign of Vijayaditya, an Early Chalukyan ruler who preceded Vikramaditya II.

The temple is associated with the Dravida style and was earlier known as Vijayeshvara.

Galaganatha and Kashi Vishweshwara Temples

The Galaganatha and Kashi Vishweshwara temples are associated with the Nagara or Rekha-Nagara tradition. Their towers demonstrate the northern form within an important southern Indian temple complex.

The presence of these temples alongside Dravida temples is one reason Pattadakal is important for understanding the interaction of architectural styles.

Pattadakal and UNESCO World Heritage status

The Group of Monuments at Pattadakal was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987.

The World Heritage property contains an important group of 9 Hindu temples and 1 Jain sanctuary. The Jain sanctuary is associated with a later Rashtrakuta phase; therefore, the entire group should not be assigned to the reign of Pulakeshin II.

UNESCO recognises the site for its architectural importance and the interaction of northern and southern temple forms.

Status as of 18 November 2026: Pattadakal is an inscribed UNESCO World Heritage property. Aihole and Badami appear in a separate Indian tentative-list proposal submitted on 9 February 2015 as a proposed extension associated with the evolution of temple architecture. A tentative-list entry is not itself a World Heritage inscription.

Connecting the 3 centres

The political and architectural achievements of the Early Chalukyas can be understood through 3 principal centres.

  • Badami or Vatapi: The principal royal capital, recognised for its 4 major rock-cut cave temples.
  • Aihole: An early centre of architectural experimentation, including the apsidal Durga Temple and the Meguti Jain Temple with Ravikirti's inscription of 634–635 CE.
  • Pattadakal: The royal coronation centre, associated with mature Nagara and Dravida temple forms and the Virupaksha Temple commissioned by Lokamahadevi around 740 CE.

Prelims focus

  • Pattadakal: Karnataka; associated with Chalukyan royal coronations.
  • Virupaksha Temple: commissioned by Queen Lokamahadevi around 740 CE.
  • Vikramaditya II: ruler whose Pallava victories were commemorated by the Virupaksha Temple.
  • Mallikarjuna Temple: Queen Trailokyamahadevi.
  • Virupaksha, Mallikarjuna and Sangameshwara: Dravida tradition.
  • Galaganatha and Kashi Vishweshwara: Nagara tradition.
  • Group of Monuments at Pattadakal: UNESCO World Heritage inscription in 1987.
  • Trap: The Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal belongs to the later reign of Vikramaditya II, not the reign of Pulakeshin II.

[NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 85–88; Archaeological Survey of India, Dharwad Circle, The Group of Monuments, sections Historical Perspective and Architectural Achievements, consulted 18 November 2026; Government of Karnataka, Department of Tourism, Mallikarjuna Temple, sections Introduction and Architectural Marvel, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Pattadakal, World Heritage List entry 239, Description and inscription information, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Evolution of Temple Architecture – Aihole-Badami-Pattadakal, Tentative List entry 5972, submission dated 9 February 2015, consulted 18 November 2026.]
